title: A1 quiz: dividers, loading, and pull-ups

items.q: Vin = 5 V, R1 (top) = 10 kΩ, R2 (bottom) = 20 kΩ, no load. What is Vout?
items.why: Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2) = 5 × 20 / 30 = 3.33 V. 1.67 V is what you get by putting R1 in the numerator by mistake (5 × 10 / 30).

items.q: A 12.6 V battery feeds a divider with R1 = 20 kΩ (top) and R2 = 10 kΩ (bottom). What voltage reaches the ADC pin?
items.why: 12.6 × 10 / (20 + 10) = 12.6 / 3 = 4.2 V, safely under the Uno's 5 V ADC range. 8.4 V is the R1-on-top-of-the-fraction mistake.

items.q: With 4.2 V on the pin, about what does the Uno's 10-bit ADC (5 V reference) read?
items.why: 4.2 / 5 × 1023 = 859.3, so about 859 (860 with the 1024 convention). 430 would be about 2.1 V; 1023 would mean the pin was at or above 5 V.

items.q: How much current does that 20k + 10k divider draw from the 12.6 V battery?
items.why: I = 12.6 V / (20 kΩ + 10 kΩ) = 0.42 mA, continuously. That's about 10 mAh per day (0.42 mA × 24 h), which matters on a battery robot.

items.q: What is the Thévenin output impedance of a 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ divider?
items.why: Rth = R1 ∥ R2 = (10k × 10k) / (10k + 10k) = 5 kΩ. Looking back into the output with Vin shorted, both resistors appear in parallel.

items.q: A 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ divider from 5 V is loaded with 10 kΩ from Vout to GND. What is Vout now?
items.why: R2 ∥ RL = 5 kΩ, so Vout = 5 × 5 / (10 + 5) = 1.67 V. Or with Thévenin: 2.5 × 10 / (5 + 10) = 1.67 V. A load equal to R2 drops the output by a third.

items.q: Same divider (Vth = 2.5 V, Rth = 5 kΩ) loaded with 50 kΩ. What is Vout?
items.why: Vout = 2.5 × 50 / (5 + 50) = 2.27 V, a 9.1% error. A load 10× Rth still costs about 9% (1/11); for precision you want 100× or a buffer.

items.q: Why does I2C need pull-up resistors?
choices: To limit the current into the microcontroller
Because the SDA and SCL outputs are open-drain: devices can only pull the line low, so something must pull it high
To filter noise at high frequencies
items.why: Open-drain lets several devices share the bus safely (no push-pull fights), enables wired-AND for ACK and clock stretching, and lets the pull-up set the logic-high voltage. Without pull-ups, the line never goes high.

items.q: An I2C line has a 4.7 kΩ pull-up to 5 V. How much current must a device sink to hold it low (near 0 V)?
items.why: I = 5 V / 4.7 kΩ = 1.06 mA, under the 3 mA the I2C spec guarantees a device can sink at 0.4 V. (To be exact, 4.6 V across the resistor gives 0.98 mA.)

items.q: Rp = 4.7 kΩ and bus capacitance Cb = 100 pF. Using t_r ≈ 0.8473 × Rp × Cb (30% to 70%), which I2C modes meet the rise-time limit?
choices: Both standard (100 kHz, 1000 ns) and fast (400 kHz, 300 ns)
items.why: t_r = 0.8473 × 4.7 kΩ × 100 pF = 398 ns. That's under 1000 ns (standard) but over 300 ns (fast). For 400 kHz, use a smaller pull-up such as 2.2 kΩ (186 ns).

items.q: What is the minimum pull-up for a 3.3 V I2C bus, if devices sink 3 mA at V_OL = 0.4 V?
items.why: Rp,min = (VCC − V_OL) / I_OL = (3.3 − 0.4) / 3 mA = 967 Ω. 1.53 kΩ is the answer for 5 V ((5 − 0.4) / 3 mA). Smaller than the minimum and a device can't pull the line low enough to read as 0.

items.q: The GY-521 pulls SDA up to 3.3 V. Using the ATmega328P general I/O V_IH of 0.6 × VCC at VCC = 5 V, what is the high-level noise margin?
items.why: V_IH = 0.6 × 5 = 3.0 V, and the line idles at 3.3 V: margin = 3.3 − 3.0 = 0.3 V. It works, but noise, long wires, or a sagging rail can eat 0.3 V. (If the TWI table's stricter 0.7 × VCC = 3.5 V applies, it's actually below spec.)

items.q: A 5 V sensor outputs a 'high' of 2.2 V into an ATmega328P input (VCC = 5 V, V_IL max = 1.5 V, V_IH min = 3.0 V). What will the pin read?
choices: Undefined: 2.2 V is between V_IL max and V_IH min, so it may read either way
items.why: Between 1.5 V and 3.0 V the datasheet guarantees nothing. It may read high on the bench and low when hot. Design to stay out of the gap.

items.q: You need the HC-SR04's 5 V ECHO signal on a 3.3 V Raspberry Pi pin. Which divider is right?
choices: 1 kΩ from ECHO to the Pi pin, 2 kΩ from the Pi pin to GND (gives 3.33 V)
2 kΩ from ECHO to the Pi pin, 1 kΩ from the Pi pin to GND (gives 1.67 V)
1 kΩ from ECHO to the Pi pin, nothing to GND
No resistors: Pi pins are 5 V tolerant
items.why: 5 × 2 / (1 + 2) = 3.33 V. Swapped gives 5 × 1 / 3 = 1.67 V, which may not read high. A series resistor alone doesn't lower the voltage on a high-impedance input. Pi GPIO is NOT 5 V tolerant.

items.q: A button goes from pin 2 to GND, with pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP). What does digitalRead(2) return while the button is pressed?
items.why: The internal pull-up holds the pin HIGH when released; pressing connects it to GND, so it reads LOW. Active-low logic: code must test for LOW to detect a press.

interview.q: How would you measure a 12 V battery with a microcontroller whose ADC only reads 0 to 5 V? Walk me through your component choices.
rubric: Uses a resistor divider, states the equation Vout = Vin × R2 / (R1 + R2), and picks a ratio that keeps the maximum battery voltage (about 12.6 V or more) below the ADC reference with margin
Discusses resistor magnitude as a trade-off: larger values waste less battery current, smaller values keep the source impedance low enough for the ADC (about 10 kΩ or less on an ATmega328P)
Mentions loading and Thévenin output impedance, and a capacitor on the ADC pin or a buffer as fixes
Explains converting the ADC count back to battery volts in firmware, including the divider ratio and calibration
Mentions protection or robustness: overvoltage on the pin, tolerances of the resistors, and noise filtering

interview.q: Why does I2C need pull-up resistors, and how do you choose their value?
rubric: Explains open-drain outputs: devices can only pull low, so the pull-up provides the high level; this allows bus sharing, ACK, and clock stretching safely
Upper limit: rise time from Rp and bus capacitance (t_r ≈ 0.85 Rp Cb), with the mode limits (about 1000 ns at 100 kHz, 300 ns at 400 kHz)
Lower limit: devices must sink the current at V_OL (3 mA at 0.4 V gives about 1.5 kΩ at 5 V)
Gives typical values (4.7 kΩ at 100 kHz, 2.2 kΩ at 400 kHz or longer wires) and notes that pull-ups on several modules add in parallel
Mentions the pull-up voltage sets the logic-high level, so it matters in mixed 3.3 V / 5 V systems

interview.q: Your MPU-6050 breakout works on the bench, but I2C reads fail intermittently once it's mounted on the robot with longer wires near the motors. How do you debug it?
rubric: Starts with measurements: scope SDA and SCL to look at rise times, high and low levels, and noise or ringing, rather than guessing
Identifies likely causes: bus capacitance from long wires slowing edges, small noise margin from 3.3 V pull-ups on a 5 V MCU, motor noise or ground bounce, a sagging supply
Proposes fixes tied to the cause: stronger pull-ups, lower bus speed, shorter or twisted wiring, a level shifter, separate grounds or decoupling for motor and logic
Mentions firmware robustness: timeouts, error counting, and bus recovery so one bad read doesn't hang the robot
Verifies the fix under the failing condition (motors running) and draws on a systematic troubleshooting process
